Question: Which resources have similar content — code, documentation or data values — and how does this one differ?
Why is this important?: Finds candidates by what they contain, including resources whose scope and purpose were never declared — the only similarity that works before any curation.
Rationale/Source: Content similarity over embeddings of code, documents and sampled data (pgvector). Two resources are similar when their descriptions are near; the evidence names which parts were near, never a retrieved chunk, and a description built under a scoped credential says so. An agent then describes how they differ from those parts. Not built; see DESIGN-BROADER-QUESTIONS-WITHOUT-CONTENT-INGESTION.md §3. Reworded 2026-09-28 (was: content similarity over pgvector embeddings).

Question: Which resources overlap with this one — the same data, a subset, a stand-in or a replacement — and how does this one differ?
Why is this important?: Whether a resource can substitute for another is a question of scope — subject, grain, coverage in time and space — not of content; this is what a consumer choosing between two datasets actually asks.
Rationale/Source: Scope similarity is lens fit (design §16.5): derive a lens from this resource's declared or measured DataScope, DataGrain and subject terms and run the fit against every other resource's stored scope — no new survey, a query over stored measurements. Runs both ways, so a resource that fails one investigation's lens can still match another (§16.5 point 5). Also the mechanism behind 'is something like this already productised' (§16.7 5′). The answer is a relation per scope axis — subject, population (which customers: pre-sales vs post-sales), space, time, grain, structure — each same / contains / contained_by / overlaps / disjoint / not_established, with 'can one stand in for the other' and 'is one a subset of the other' derived from them (design §16.8). Two 'customer' databases are never called similar on subject alone: an undeclared population axis renders not_established. Absorbs Q-0009 (replace or extend something we already have) as the stand-in and replacement clause, and Q-0010 (similar content) as evidence for the same relation; Q-0070 stays at container level as the structural-signature evidence for databases and file systems.
Answering Analysis: MIXED: preliminary_fit + coverage_signals + subject_signals + grain_determination (the lens is derived from a resource rather than an investigation — design §16.5 'lens from a resource'; the comparison is requirement_fit's field-by-field overlap); for repositories and file systems the same question is a registry query over already-registered resources and a description-embedding similarity, neither of which is built (absorbed from Q-0009 and Q-0010)
Catalog History: 2026-09-26: split from 'What are similar resources, and how does this differ?' Why is this important?: Whether a survey can run at all, and where it runs, decides the cost and the provenance of every answer that follows.

Question: Where is this resource physically located, under which jurisdiction, and are there residency or transfer constraints?
Why is this important?: Data sovereignty decides whether we may hold or process this at all, independently of what the license permits.
Rationale/Source: Two halves. The machine half reads host and region from the connection endpoint, cloud instance metadata, or the mount and file path. The human half — legal controller, residency rule — comes through Enrichment. The result is published as a proposed Egeria DataScope classification carrying scopeElements {jurisdiction, region, controller}.
Answering Analysis: GAP: nothing populates DataScope from a survey today; endpoint geolocation and the Enrichment section are both unbuilt.

Question: What is the scope of the data in time — collection period, validity and coverage?
Why is this important?: A consumer needs to know which period the data actually covers before trusting any answer drawn from it.
Rationale/Source: The other half of DataScope, and machine-proposable for most types: minimum and maximum of date columns for a database, modification-time range and in-file date ranges for a filesystem, DCAT temporal for a published dataset. Human confirmation of validity and coverage comes through Enrichment.
Answering Analysis: MIXED: coverage_signals (Discovery, catalog tier — partition bounds, file-name dates, descriptor temporal fields; identity A) + coverage_profile (Analysis, data identity B — measured date ranges, cadence and gaps per table); the declared DataScope is curated from the measured one (design §16, §14)

Why is this important?: The demand half: building a data product nobody asked for costs more than it returns.

Question: How big is this database — schemas, tables, views, columns, rows and bytes?
Why is this important?: Size sets the cost of every later tier, and is the first thing that says whether this is a toy or a production estate.
Rationale/Source: Whole-database catalog reads only, no row data: information_schema and pg_catalog give the structural counts, and relation sizes plus row counts give the volume. Design §5.1 — extract everything the catalog already knows before reading a row.
Answering Analysis: MIXED: schema_inventory (structural counts) + row_count_snapshot (rows and bytes)

Question: Which schemas carry the data, and which are system, empty or staging?
Why is this important?: Knowing which schemas matter stops every later analysis from paying to profile scratch and system objects.
Rationale/Source: Derived from the same catalog read as the size question — object counts and sizes per schema, plus name conventions. Cheap, whole-database, no row data.
Answering Analysis: schema_inventory

Question: Is this database alive — writes since the statistics were reset, last vacuum or analyse, and is anything reading it?
Why is this important?: A database nobody writes to and nobody reads is a retirement candidate, not a survey candidate.
Rationale/Source: pg_stat_user_tables carries n_tup_ins/upd/del, n_live_tup, n_dead_tup, last_vacuum/autovacuum/analyze, seq_scan and idx_scan; pg_stat_database carries the transaction and block counters. All of it is a catalog read. Note the two absence modes design §5.1 calls out: a counter the engine does not support is not_established, and statistics that were never collected must render as "run ANALYZE", not as "no activity".
Answering Analysis: db_activity_signals (design §5.2, §5.7 — database-wide roll-up of pg_stat_user_tables tuple and scan counters; reuses postgres_schema_and_stats' per-table figures rather than re-querying them)

Question: Is this database documented — what fraction of its tables and columns carry comments?
Why is this important?: Undocumented tables are the single biggest obstacle to anyone reusing a database they did not build.
Rationale/Source: pg_description via obj_description and col_description gives comments per table and per column; the measure is coverage, not presence. Note rule 13 in the package CLAUDE.md — these need the schema-qualified (schema.table)::regclass form.
Answering Analysis: GAP: nothing measures comment coverage across a database's tables and columns. Design §5.2 proposes a new database comment-coverage analysis; its proposed id is deliberately not spelled out in this note, because it contains a readable repo analysis id as a substring and the stale-gap guard matches on substrings.

Question: What engine and version is this, which extensions are installed, and is the version still supported?
Why is this important?: An unsupported engine version is a security and upgrade liability before anything about the data matters.
Rationale/Source: Server-level rather than database-level — design §5 makes server, database, schema and table each addressable, and this row belongs to the server subset. Sources: version(), pg_settings, pg_extension, and the upstream support window for the major version.
Answering Analysis: GAP: db_server_profile (proposed, server-level) — no analysis reads pg_settings, pg_extension or the version support window.

Question: Is this database a primary or a replica, is it clustered, and is WAL archiving or backup configured?
Why is this important?: Whether the data survives a failure is a property of the deployment, not of the schema, and nothing else in a survey reveals it.
Rationale/Source: Catalog-observable: pg_is_in_recovery() for the primary/standby role, pg_stat_replication for standbys and replay lag, pg_settings.archive_mode with pg_stat_archiver for WAL archiving, pg_extension and roles for backup tooling such as pgBackRest, barman or wal-g, Citus catalogs for clustering. Design §5.5 — last successful backup and tested restore are NOT observable and are asked separately.
Answering Analysis: db_resilience (design §5.5, MIXED — catalog half measured directly: primary/standby, replicas and lag, WAL archiving status, backup-tool/Citus-clustering signals; Enrichment half stays explicitly pending, never silently omitted)

Question: When was this resource last backed up successfully, and has a restore ever been tested?
Why is this important?: These are the two resilience questions a data owner actually asks, and the two that nothing inside the resource itself can answer.
Rationale/Source: Design §5.5 draws the line explicitly for databases: primary/standby role, replicas, WAL archiving and extension-based backup tooling are catalog-observable, while last successful backup, tested restore and RPO/RTO are not, for any resource type. They come from an Enrichment "Backup and recovery" section, and the answer envelope must say which half answered.
Answering Analysis: MIXED: db_resilience (machine half — backup-tool signals and WAL archiving status, explicitly non-definitive: absence of a detected tool is not absence of backups) + human-supplied via the Enrichment Context form (last successful backup, last tested restore, RPO/RTO)
Catalog History: 2026-09-26: moved to Enrichment (project owner, live review): the definitive answer is human; db_resilience's backup-tool signal is shown as non-definitive supporting evidence.

Question: What kind of database is this — transactional, analytical, reference data, staging or a copy?
Why is this important?: The kind of database decides which later analyses are worth paying for at all.
Rationale/Source: Zero new fetch — reasons over what Scouting already stored: table shapes, foreign-key density, naming conventions, read/write ratios from the tuple counters, and the query mix if pg_stat_statements is installed.
Answering Analysis: db_classification (design §5.3, §5.7 — derived from stored table shapes, key/FK density, naming patterns and the read/write mix in stored tuple counters; confidence scales with how many signal families were available)

Question: Is there a data model here — do the tables relate through foreign keys, or is this a bag of tables?
Why is this important?: A database with no declared relationships needs a very different kind of attention from one with a real model.
Rationale/Source: Zero new fetch: the foreign-key constraints Scouting already read become a graph, and the measure is connectivity — orphan tables, components, in-degree.
Answering Analysis: db_relationship_graph (design §5.3, §5.7 — builds the FK graph from stored column rows: edge count, connected components, isolated tables, most-referenced tables)

Question: What is the grain of each table — one row per what?
Why is this important?: Grain is the first thing a consumer has to know and the last thing most databases write down.
Rationale/Source: Inferred from primary-key composition, column names, n_distinct approaching the row count, and date columns — emitted as an Egeria DataGrainAnnotation with a grainStatement and a confidence. Shared with the filesystem path, where the same inference runs over a data file's columns.
Answering Analysis: grain_determination (design §5.3, §5.7 — derived from the declared primary key, or a stored column profile whose distinct count matches the row count, plus any date column in the key; extended 2026-09-24 with §16.3's time grain from naming — a period word or date-shaped suffix in the table name, or a column named like a date whatever its type — each interval carrying the basis it came from and a confidence for it, so a key-declared period is no longer indistinguishable from a guess about a naming habit; published as a DataGrainAnnotation proposal)
Catalog History: 2026-09-24: extended with multi-resource-questions-design.md §16.3's time grain from naming (table-name period words, Postgres child-partition date suffixes, date-named columns of non-temporal type), each with an explicit interval_basis and interval_confidence. The entity-grain-from-keys half of §16.2 was already built and is unchanged. §16.2's literal year=/month=/day= partition keys are a filesystem layout and are not looked for here.

Question: Is this a copy, subset or superset of a resource we already know — structurally, by schema or file signature?
Why is this important?: Paying to survey, host and govern the third copy of the same database is a cost nobody decided to take on.

Read from the stored table-activity rows; no new fetch. Never analyzed (Postgres NULL) and not read are kept apart.

Question: What is the full schema — tables, columns, types, keys, constraints and indexes?
Why is this important?: The schema is the contract, and every structural question downstream is asked against it.
Rationale/Source: The complete catalog read: information_schema and pg_catalog for schemas, tables, columns and types; pg_constraint for primary, foreign, unique and check constraints; pg_index for indexes. Published under Egeria's own Relational* metric keys so a native and a local run are comparable (design §2.2).
Answering Analysis: schema_inventory

Question: What do the columns actually contain — nulls, distinct counts, most-common values, ranges and widths?
Why is this important?: Types say what a column may hold; only the values say what it does hold.
Rationale/Source: pg_stats, populated by ANALYZE, already carries null_frac, n_distinct, most_common_vals, most_common_freqs, histogram_bounds, avg_width and correlation — column profiling with no sampling at all. Value sampling is the fallback for columns whose statistics are stale or missing. Design §5.8: the answer envelope must state which route ran and, when sampled, the strategy, bound and seed.
Answering Analysis: PARTIAL: value_profile supplies the measured half — per-column record, value, distinct and null counts, empty and placeholder-text counts and date bounds over the whole table, with no sampling. Most-common values, widths and ranges from pg_stats (with bounded sampling where pg_stats is absent) are stored by the column-profile step (Phase 1 slice 10) but no analysis id reads them back into this answer; data_class_match and reference_data_match consume them for their own questions.
Catalog History: 2026-10-22: names value_profile, the catalogue id, instead of the postgres_column_profile step (review §2).

Question: Which columns conform to a known Data Class, with what confidence, and which look like a class we do not have yet?
Why is this important?: Knowing where the sensitive data actually sits is the precondition for every privacy and access question after it.
Rationale/Source: Generalises the existing PII matching: column name, type and sampled value patterns matched against every Egeria DataClass, producing a DataClassAnnotation per column with a stated confidence. Columns that show a clear pattern but match nothing raise an RFA proposing a new Data Class, carrying the observed pattern. Per design §5.8 the confidence is always stated against the sample, never as an unqualified "conforms".
Answering Analysis: data_class_match (Phase 1 slice 10, design §5.4/§5.8 — matches column name, type and bounded value sampling against every Egeria DataClass the platform holds, producing a DataClassAnnotation per column; an unmatched-but-patterned column is proposed as a new DataClass with contentStatus: DRAFT, linked to its evidence via AssociatedAnnotation)
Catalog History: 2026-10-22: `dataset` withdrawn from Resource Types until a dataset surveyor exists (review §1.1).

Question: Which low-cardinality columns conform to a known reference-data set, and which should become one?
Why is this important?: Uncontrolled code columns are where data quality quietly fails, and they are cheap to find.
Rationale/Source: Columns whose n_distinct falls under a threshold have their distinct values compared against every Egeria ValidValueSet. A full match becomes ValidValuesAssignment advice; a partial match raises an RFA listing the unmatched values; no match at all raises an RFA proposing a new ValidValueSet carrying the values.
Answering Analysis: reference_data_match (design §5.4 — compares each low-cardinality column's sampled distinct values against every Egeria ValidValueSet: a full match becomes ValidValuesAssignment advice, a partial match raises an RFA listing the unmatched values, and no match at all proposes a new ValidValueSet carrying the values)

Question: Which columns hold semi-structured data (JSON, JSONB, XML, arrays or hstore), and what is inside them — keys, nesting, types and consistency across rows?
Why is this important?: A schema that stops at "jsonb" describes the column and says nothing about the data.
Rationale/Source: JSONB via jsonb_object_keys and jsonb_typeof over a bounded sample, giving key frequency, nesting depth and type consistency across rows; XML via the root element and xpath key sampling. The result is a SchemaAnalysisAnnotation carrying an inferred nested schema, sharing its inference core with the filesystem path's JSON and XML file profiling. Absorbs Q-0074's first clause: which columns hold semi-structured data comes from the column types already in the catalog read, at zero new fetch; the share of stored bytes they account for is the part nothing measures.
Answering Analysis: PARTIAL: nested_column_profile (design §5.4/§5.7, postgres_nested_columns — classifies the JSON/JSONB/XML/array/hstore columns from the stored column types, then samples them and infers a nested schema: per-key presence frequency and JSON-type consistency, or for XML the root element and element/attribute name frequency, plus nesting depth). Remaining gap, from the first clause: the share of stored bytes those columns account for is not measured by any analysis.
Catalog History: 2026-10-22: stage widened to Discovery/Analysis; absorbs Q-0074 ('Which columns hold semi-structured data ..., and how much of the data sits in them?') as its first clause (review §1.6); the bytes-share remainder is the PARTIAL gap.

Question: Which tables have no primary key, no foreign key, no comment, unused indexes, or names that break the convention?
Why is this important?: These are the specific, fixable defects behind a vague sense that a database is badly kept.
Rationale/Source: Check-granular in the same shape as the repository conventions analysis: each defect is its own named check so an assessment can cite it and a subscription can watch it. All of it reads the catalog, including pg_stat_user_indexes for indexes nothing uses.
Answering Analysis: schema_conventions (design §5.4, §5.7 — check-granular structural hygiene derived from stored rows: no primary key, no foreign key, no comment, non-snake_case names; does not cover unused indexes, which needs a live pg_stat_user_indexes read)

Question: What does this database depend on outside itself — foreign data wrappers, dblink, extensions or publications?
Why is this important?: An external dependency is a reachability, security and upgrade constraint that the schema alone never shows.
Rationale/Source: pg_foreign_server and pg_foreign_table for FDWs, pg_extension for extensions including dblink, pg_publication and pg_subscription for logical replication. A catalog read, no row data.
Answering Analysis: db_external_dependencies (design §5.4 — extensions, foreign data wrappers/servers/tables, logical replication publications/subscriptions)
Catalog History: 2026-10-22: Purpose Integrate added (owner ruling 2026-10-13; review §1.7).

Question: Who can read and write what — roles, grants, superusers, PUBLIC grants — which sensitive columns can which roles read, and what has changed?
Why is this important?: Access is only half an answer; access crossed with sensitivity is the half anyone acts on.
Rationale/Source: pg_roles, role_table_grants and pg_default_acl give the access half and already have an analysis. The sensitivity half needs column-level Data Class matching, and the question is the cross of the two — which is why a broad PUBLIC grant on an unremarkable table and the same grant on a table of personal data read identically today. Absorbs Q-0089 (the scored sensitive-data exposure): sensitive columns identified by Data Class matching, crossed with who holds read access to them, weighted by the breadth of the grant.
Answering Analysis: PARTIAL: privilege_audit answers the roles, grants, superuser and PUBLIC-grant half; grant_change names what changed between the two most recent surveys (new grants, especially to PUBLIC, and revoked ones); the sensitive-column half (which sensitive columns can which roles read, absorbed from Q-0089) needs the columns data_class_match matched crossed with the grants, and nothing crosses the two today.
Catalog History: 2026-10-22: absorbs Q-0089 ('What is the sensitive-data exposure — which sensitive columns can which roles read?') as its last clause (review §1.6); names grant_change for 'and what changed'; data_class_match is built (catalogued, queued), so the old note's 'proposed' is corrected — the join between it and the grants is what is not built.

Question: How is this database changing — rows inserted, updated and deleted per table per period, size drift and schema churn?
Why is this important?: A point-in-time survey cannot distinguish a busy table from an abandoned one; the deltas can.
Rationale/Source: Deltas of the n_tup_ins/upd/del counters and of relation sizes between two stored snapshots, per table, producing a series the Understanding tier can chart and the change detectors in design §9 can threshold. Depends on the structured per-snapshot tables, not on re-parsing the survey JSON blob.
Answering Analysis: db_change_rates (design §5.4, §5.7 — rows inserted/updated/deleted per table per period, size drift and table-level schema churn, differenced between two stored survey snapshots) + schema_diff (column-level drift: columns added, dropped or retyped, between the two most recent surveys)
Catalog History: 2026-10-22: names schema_diff for the schema-churn clause (review §2).

Question: Which glossary terms do these columns probably mean?
Why is this important?: Columns bound to agreed terms are the difference between a catalogued database and an understandable one.
Rationale/Source: Suggestions rather than assignments, drawn from column names, any matched Data Classes and any matched reference-data sets, and published as Egeria SemanticAnnotations for a steward to accept or reject.
Answering Analysis: GAP: semantic suggestions (a proposed capability — registered 2026-09-29 as the stub catalog id semantic-suggestions, ENRICHMENT-E1-CONTEXT-TAB, not implemented) — the vocabulary layer: match column names and the stored column-profile evidence (distinct ratio, patterns, top values, sampled under the credential's budget) against Egeria glossary terms and data classes, proposing SemanticAnnotations for a person to confirm in Enrichment; no row is read beyond the profile's sample. SemanticAnnotation exists as a type and nothing produces one yet: the stub is a placeholder registration only, gated on a confirmed glossary term, with no runner behind it. See DESIGN-BROADER-QUESTIONS-WITHOUT-CONTENT-INGESTION.md §2. Reworded 2026-09-28.

Question: How complete and consistent is this database's documentation — what fraction of its tables and columns carry comments?
Why is this important?: Documentation coverage is the scored version of the Scouting comment question, and the one a steward is measured on.
Rationale/Source: Scores the coverage measure against criteria and adds the convention checks — a database where every table has a comment but half of them repeat the table name is not well documented.
Answering Analysis: PARTIAL: schema_conventions supplies the completeness half (tables and columns with no comment, banded against nothing-captured — the comment coverage Q-0063 asked for, answered today under the wrong label); doc_evidence_check, a catalogue placeholder that is not built, is the consistency half, reading ingested documentation for evidence. No analysis yet scores comment quality (e.g. a comment that only repeats the table name).
Catalog History: 2026-10-22: absorbs Q-0063 ('Is this database documented — what fraction of its tables and columns carry comments?'): schema_conventions already counts tables and columns with no comment, so it was answered under the wrong label; doc_evidence_check named for the consistency half (review §1.6).

Question: What is the sensitive-data exposure — which sensitive columns can which roles read?
Why is this important?: This is the question a privacy review actually asks, and it is a cross of two analyses rather than either one.
Rationale/Source: The scored form of the access-and-sensitivity question in Analysis: sensitive columns identified by Data Class matching, crossed with who holds read access to them, weighted by the breadth of the grant. A PUBLIC grant on a column of personal data is the finding this exists to surface.
Answering Analysis: PARTIAL: privilege_audit supplies who can read what; the sensitive-column half needs the proposed data_class_match, and nothing crosses the two today.
Catalog History: 2026-10-22: merged into Q-0085 (REVIEW-QUESTIONS-AND-ANALYTICS-2026-10-22 §2); the row is kept so the id is never reused.

Question: How well-modelled is this database — keys, constraints, foreign-key coverage, orphan tables and grain clarity?
Why is this important?: Modelling quality predicts how expensive this database will be to integrate with anything else.
Rationale/Source: Scores the convention checks together with grain clarity: a table whose grain cannot be stated is a modelling defect even when its constraints are all present.
Answering Analysis: MIXED: schema_conventions (keys and constraints -- tables with no primary key, tables with no foreign key) + db_relationship_graph (foreign-key coverage, connected components, isolated/orphan tables) + grain_determination (per-table grain clarity, or a named modelling gap where none exists)

Question: How well-governed is this database's reference data — what share of its low-cardinality columns are bound to a set?
Why is this important?: Reference-data governance is measurable as a share, which makes it one of the few governance claims that can be tracked over time.
Rationale/Source: The denominator is the columns whose cardinality makes them reference-data candidates; the numerator is those bound to an Egeria ValidValueSet. Both come from the reference-data matching analysis.
Answering Analysis: PARTIAL: reference_data_match supplies the per-column checks (built, not proposed) -- which columns are low-cardinality, and whether each is matched, partially matched or unmatched against a ValidValueSet -- but nothing aggregates those verdicts into the governance share this question asks for.

Question: Is this database maintained and healthy — vacuum recency, dead-tuple ratio and unused indexes?
Why is this important?: Operational neglect shows up in the statistics long before it shows up as an outage.
Rationale/Source: Scores the activity signals against thresholds: how long since the last vacuum or analyze, the ratio of dead to live tuples, and indexes that have never been scanned. Remember design §5.1's absence rule — statistics that were never collected must not read as a healthy zero.
Answering Analysis: db_activity_signals (design §5.2, §5.7 — vacuum recency and dead-tuple ratios read from the same stored pg_stat_user_tables figures as the activity-signals roll-up above)

Question: Is this database resilient — replica present, archiving on, backup evidence and a tested restore?
Why is this important?: A data owner signing off on a database is signing off on its recovery, not its schema.
Rationale/Source: Design §5.5 makes this deliberately two-sided: the catalog facts (role, replicas, archiving, backup tooling) and the Enrichment facts (last successful backup, tested restore, RPO and RTO). The envelope must say which half answered, because a green score drawn only from the catalog half would claim something nobody verified.
Answering Analysis: db_resilience (design §5.5, MIXED — combines the catalog-read half above with an Enrichment 'Backup and recovery' section that stays explicitly pending rather than silently omitted)

Question: What kinds of files does this filesystem contain, and how much data is there?
Why is this important?: Need a basic inventory before deciding whether deeper analysis of this filesystem is worth the time.
Rationale/Source: File walk classifies every file by format and type, records sizes and timestamps — RE's baseline inventory for a filesystem resource, the filesystem equivalent of schema_inventory for a database.
Answering Analysis: filesystem_inventory

Question: Which data-quality checks should this database have?
Why is this important?: A data owner cannot ask for quality until someone says what to check, and writing the checks by hand for hundreds of tables never gets done.
Rationale/Source: propose_quality_checks reads the measured value profile and, for every column and table, applies the selection rules to propose a check, each in an Egeria quality dimension: Completeness (is the value there: Required, Missing_Pct, Required_No_Placeholder and Row_Ct_Pct), Uniqueness (Unique), Timeliness (Future_Date) and Conformity (Min_Date). A person accepts or rejects each proposal in Curate; a check whose inputs were not measured is listed as not established with the reason, never silently left out.
Answering Analysis: quality_checks (the propose_quality_checks step)
Catalog History: 2026-10-21: added with quality slice Q2 (the DatabaseQualitySurvey definition); the Q2 live test found the survey was not offered because no catalog question was scoped to it.

Question: Which data-quality checks hold on this database's tables, and which fail?
Why is this important?: A check nobody runs is a wish; the steward needs to see which accepted checks pass, warn or fail, and which could not be evaluated.
Rationale/Source: run_quality_checks runs the checks a person accepted, one aggregate query per table, and records pass, warning or fail per check, or not established with the reason (an empty table, a zero baseline, a column that has gone) and never a pass for a measure that is undefined. Each evaluated check is published as one Egeria QualityAnnotation in its dimension: Completeness (is the value there: Required, Missing_Pct, Required_No_Placeholder and Row_Ct_Pct), Uniqueness (Unique), Timeliness (Future_Date) and Conformity (Min_Date). With no accepted check the step is not run ("no accepted checks"), never an empty report.
Answering Analysis: quality_checks (the run_quality_checks step; it runs the checks accepted in Curate)
Catalog History: 2026-10-21: added with quality slice Q2 (the DatabaseQualitySurvey definition); see Q-0096.

Why is this important?: A survey that cannot see a schema reports it as empty; knowing what the credential can read first says which later answers are measured and which are blind.
